name: exp3-iter1-speed-repair
description: "Why exp3 iter_1 candidates timed out (1 core, load ~20, 170 ms/eval; dsum_decay ESS 28) and the width-grouped Chebyshev trick that made location_biased_range_prior ~9 min/chain"
metadata:

---

Exp3 iter_1 (2026-11-01): every candidate built on graded_prior_digit_sum_concepts was rejected as too slow. Admission runs warm-start NUTS at target_accept 0.99 with 3000 tune + 4000 draws per chain, under a 30-minute limit per sampling run, on 1 core at load ~20.
- The incumbent-style graph (Chebyshev in kappa over sets x 5050 ranges, plus a posterior @ membership matmul) costs ~170 ms per eval. The cumsum-over-(lo,hi)-grid trick was slower (gathers and cumsums on 154x10000 arrays are memory-bound).
- dsum_decay is barely identified (posterior sd 0.6 vs prior 1, ESS 28) and funnels against the digit-sum family weight. This is the geometry problem behind the graded models.
- Fix (candidate_1_repair_1): drop centre weighting and dsum_decay. Range log-likelihoods are then constant, so in prepare_observed precompute per set, and per observed (set, target) cell, sums over the ranges of each width of exp(ll - max) times Chebyshev coefficients of exp(slope*u) in the slope. In the graph that becomes cells x 100 x 8 contractions: 12 ms per eval, 16 steps, 0.08 s per iteration, about 9 min per chain. Verified exact against brute force.
- Location slope posterior 0.13 ± 0.36. Prediction RMSE vs centre_weighted_ranges_digit_sums (kappa posterior mean 0.039) ≈ 0.0037.
**How to apply:** for exp3 candidates, time the gradient (logp_dlogp_function) and a 600-iteration warm-start run before submitting; avoid parameters such as dsum_decay that the data barely constrain. See [[exp3-iter1-saturation-probes]].

description: exp3 iter_1 cand_0 (2026-11-01) MAP probes on graded_prior_digit_sum_concepts (MAP -3513.54) — target-as-evidence, previous-set carry-over, random-generator program, odd own family, kind-level sharpening all pin at normative
metadata:

---
Base graded_prior_digit_sum_concepts, MAP LL -3513.54 on exp3 (family weights: parity .025, special .152, multiples .125, ends .142, contains ~0, exceptions ~0, digit sums .025, ranges .53; scale 79, centre .017, dsum_decay -0.25).
- Target as partial evidence (positive test, boost (P(t|h)/P(t|noise))^w): w 0.006, no gain.
- Carry-over of the previous different set's family posterior (sequential priming): log-share power and linear blend both optimal at 0; even 0.02 blend costs 3 nats.
- Explicit "random generator" program with learned per-example typicality: weight 0, typicality 0.
- Odd and even as separate families: no gain (odd .013); removing odd costs 230 nats.
- Two-stage inference (sharpen across kinds, Bayes within): exponent 1.03, +0.4 nats.
- Incumbent aggregates are calibrated (inside/below-min/near-last/odd-set-even-target etc. all |z|<1.6).
- PROBE BUG to avoid: model.compile_fn(model["p_yes"]) draws random RVs; wrap with model.replace_rvs_by_values first.
**How to apply:** the exp3 normative concept learner is saturated on decision-, sequence- and target-side mechanisms too. See [[exp3-decision-rule-probes]], [[exp3-concept-family-probes]].

description: Exp3 iter_1 cand_1 MAP probes on graded_prior_digit_sum_concepts (LL -3513.54) — decades, geometric seqs, digit gaps, "anything" concept, odd/even split all dead; range-location slope +0.18 (submitted); incumbent at noise ceiling
metadata:

- Saturated-cell half-deviance 646 over 1227 cells (median 5 obs) ≈ noise level, so at most a few tens of nats are left to gain. Calibration gain ≈1 in every trial_index block, no drift.

- Multiples of 13-50 family +0.34 (sibling cand_2 took it). Range-location prior exp(slope*midpoint) within width: slope +0.27, +0.18, RMSE 0.004 → submitted as location_biased_range_prior.

People infer the hidden program as a Bayesian concept learner over number rules
(a prior mass per family shared equally by its members, exception rules in
their own family, digit-sum rules "digits add up to s" as a family) and the 5,050 ranges of 1..100 (an
Erlang prior on width, the size principle, 10% of examples uniform noise). The
one claim: a range's prior plausibility is not the same wherever it sits on
the number line. People expect a magnitude-based program to live in a
particular region, so among ranges of the same width the prior rises or falls
exponentially with the range's midpoint, with direction and strength
(loc_slope) inferred from the data. Magnitude generalisation is therefore
asymmetric: after a single example or a tight cluster, targets on the favoured
side are endorsed more than equally distant targets on the other side, where
the best model generalises symmetrically.

Speed: interval likelihoods do not depend on parameters, so prepare_observed
precomputes, per set (and per observed set-target cell), sums over the ranges
of each width of exp(log-likelihood) times the Chebyshev coefficients of
exp(loc_slope * u) in loc_slope (u = scaled midpoint; degree 7 on |slope| <= 3,
relative error ~2e-5). The graph then works on (cells x 100 widths x 8) arrays
instead of (sets x 5050 ranges).

import pymc as pm

NUMBERS = np.arange(1, 101)
DEG = 7
SLOPE_RANGE = 3.0

    rules = {

        "primes": [n for n in NUMBERS if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))],
        "squares": [n * n for n in range(1, 11)],
        "cubes": [n**3 for n in range(1, 5)],
        "powers of 2, not 32": [2, 4, 8, 16, 64],
        "powers of 2, or 37": [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64],
        "even": list(range(2, 101, 2)),
    }
    rules.update({f"multiples of {m}": list(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]})
    rules.update({f"powers of {m}": [m**k for k in range(1, 8) if m**k <= 100] for m in range(2, 11)})
    rules.update({f"ends in {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if n % 10 == d] for d in range(10)})
    rules.update({f"contains digit {d}": [n for n in NUMBERS if str(d) in str(n)] for d in range(10)})
    rules.update({f"digit sum {t}": [n for n in NUMBERS if sum(map(int, str(n))) == t] for t in range(1, 19)})

    if name.startswith("multiples"):
        return 2
    if name.startswith("ends"):
